Many families lived there for generations, and some still do today. The local economy depended on agriculture, fishing, and later on manufacturing. Factories were built near the water, and workers moved in from the countryside. Wages were low, and conditions were hard, but the work was steady. By the middle of the century, the population had doubled. New houses were built, and old ones were torn down. The railway arrived, and with it came new opportunities. Merchants opened shops, and banks lent money to young businesses. The town council debated taxes, roads, and water supply. Some residents complained, while others praised the progress. Newspapers reported on every meeting, and readers argued in the letters pages. In the following decades, the factories began to close. Jobs were lost, and many young people left. The town shrank, but it did not disappear. Tourists began to visit, drawn by the old buildings and the scenery. Restaurants opened, and hotels were renovated. Today, the town is quiet, but it is not forgotten. Visitors walk along the river, and they read the plaques on the walls.
